units: the steam produced while cooking drifts through the room
on contact with the cold glass this steam turns back into water
the film of water on the pane hides the view outside
the condensed water runs down and gathers at the bottom of the window
standing water swells the timber and lifts the paint
an unpleasant smell eventually spreads through the kitchen
the source of the trouble is the damp produced inside the home
letting fresh air through while cooking breaks the process
it is better to open before the film appears than afterwards
text: Steam rising from a pan does not simply vanish. It drifts across the room until it meets the cold surface of the glass, where it turns back into water and settles as a thick film that hides the street outside. Those droplets slide downwards and gather along the bottom of the frame. Left to sit, the water swells the timber, lifts the paint in blisters, and a sour smell soon spreads through the kitchen. The cause lies indoors, not in the weather: it is the damp air that cooking itself produces. Letting fresh air through while the pan is on the heat breaks the chain, since the moist air leaves, drier air takes its place, and nothing is left for the condensation to feed on. A careful occupant therefore opens the window before the panes turn white, rather than afterwards, once the damage has taken hold.

units: a sharp knock came each time the kitchen cupboard was shut
the door struck the upright instead of settling flush against it
the tenant first suspected that the timber had warped
sanding the edge down changed nothing
a lamp held close revealed play in the top hinge
the screws turned freely in holes worn too wide
splinters of wood set in glue gave the screws a firm grip again
once the glue had set the screws went back into fresh material
the door closes silently once more
the episode shows that the source of a noise rarely lies where the ear puts it
text: A sharp knock came every evening as the kitchen cupboard was shut: the left door struck the upright instead of settling flush against it. The tenant blamed the timber first, certain that damp had warped it, and sanded the edge down. Nothing changed. Then she held a lamp close and saw the trouble at once, since the top hinge had worked loose. Two screws turned freely in holes worn wide, and the panel hung slightly askew. The remedy came from an old cabinetmaker's trick: pack the tired holes with splinters of wood set in glue, leave them overnight, then drive the screws into fresh material. Since that evening the door closes without a sound. What she took from it was a small rule of thumb, namely that when a piece of furniture complains, the source rarely lies where the ear puts it.

units: the two cleaning cloths do not serve the same purpose
the kitchen cloth is thin and dries without leaving smears
the kitchen cloth suits plates and cooking surfaces
the floor cloth soaks up a large puddle
the floor cloth leaves a damp film behind it
the two must be stored apart
the floor cloth is rinsed in scalding water after use or it will smell
the kitchen cloth goes into the machine with the rest of the washing
the test for choosing is contact with food
text: Want to clean quickly and properly? Begin by distinguishing your two helpers, because they are not intended for the same job. The tea towel is thin and closely woven. It soaks up little, yet it dries without leaving smears, so keep it for plates, glasses and the hob. The floor cloth is thick and loose. It swallows a whole puddle, but it leaves a damp film behind it, hence its place on the tiles and never on the table. Store the two well apart, one folded in a drawer, the other hung over the bucket. Rinse the floor cloth in scalding water after every use, or it will begin to smell. The tea towel goes into the machine with the sheets. And if the rest escapes you, remember this: ask whether the surface touches food. If it does, reach for the towel; if not, reach for the other.

units: a voluntary group have set up a repair workshop in a disused market hall
a first bench is given over to clothing and fabric goods
trousers are taken up there and worn hems are stitched again
a second bench deals with electrical appliances
damaged power leads make up most of the electrical requests
a third bench looks after furniture
legs are glued back on there and hinges or handles are replaced
a fourth corner lends tools out for a modest membership
the queue has not shortened since the doors opened
a travelling scheme is planned for the outlying districts
text: In a disused market hall, a voluntary group have opened a workshop where things once thrown out are mended instead. The first bench takes in clothing and fabric goods: trousers are taken up, worn hems are stitched again, a torn bag strap is put right. The second deals with electrical appliances, and damaged power leads account for most of what comes through the door. The third, noticeably louder, is given over to furniture, where a chair leg is glued back on, a hinge is eased, a fresh handle is fitted. A fourth corner, quieter than the rest, lends tools out to anyone paying a modest membership. The queue, as the volunteers point out, has not shortened since the doors opened, which suggests the skill is missed more than the will. A travelling scheme is soon to serve the outlying districts.

units: at sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone
washing done the evening before hangs on a line strung between two walls
the water dripping from the washing runs into a groove cut in the ground
by the middle of the day the air dries and the sheets fill out
a cat settles on the warm rim of the well
a wooden shutter bangs on an upper floor before falling back against the wall
late in the afternoon a neighbour comes to fetch her washing
she leaves the pegs on the line
in the evening the courtyard empties and a smell of soap lingers
the night brings the damp back to the flagstones
text: At sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone. Washing hung out the evening before still sags on a line strung between two walls, and the drips fall one by one into a groove cut along the paving. By the middle of the day the air has dried, the sheets fill out and crack like sails. A grey cat settles on the warm rim of the well and half closes its eyes. Somewhere above, a wooden shutter bangs, holds open for a moment, then falls back against the wall. Late in the afternoon a neighbour comes down for her washing, folds each piece over her arm and leaves the pegs where they are, biting on the empty line. As evening comes the courtyard empties, and only the smell of soap hangs on between the walls. Then the night brings the damp back to the flagstones, and the round quietly begins again.

units: welding a casing shut instead of screwing it down blocks access to the parts inside
with no access the independent workshop cannot diagnose the fault
with no diagnosis no quote is offered
the owner ends up buying a replacement appliance
each step of the reasoning looks sound taken on its own
the sequence leads to scrapping an object that a minor part would have saved
as repairers grow scarce the passing on of practical skill is cut off
the knowledge is missing where the demand is rising
effective action bears on design and not on the sorting of waste
text: Refusing to repair costs more than it appears to, and the mechanism deserves a careful description. A maker who welds a casing shut instead of screwing it down removes all access to the parts inside. With no access, the independent workshop cannot diagnose the fault. With no diagnosis, it will not quote. With no quote, the owner buys a replacement. Every link looks sound on its own, and the chain as a whole ends with an object scrapped when a hinge or a seal would have kept it in service. A second effect follows, harder to see: as repairers grow scarce, the passing on of practical skill dries up, so the knowledge is missing exactly where the demand is rising. Turning this round therefore means acting at the design stage, and not at the far end, over the sorting of waste.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the alterations seamstress keeps a narrow shop in a district
she began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop
she assembled linings there one after another
the closing of that workshop left her without work
she owned only a second-hand machine and had no customers
she changed scale by mending single pieces instead of producing runs
each repair costs less than a replacement garment
her order book now runs two weeks ahead
she is handing the trade on to an apprentice
text: Behind a narrow shopfront, the alterations seamstress of the district practises a trade that many had written off. She began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop, assembling linings one after another along the production line. When that workshop shut its doors she was left without work, owning nothing but a second-hand machine and not a single customer. Her answer was to change scale. Rather than sewing runs of identical pieces, she offered to rescue garments one at a time. A hem taken up, a sandal strap stitched back, a torn pocket closed, a zip replaced: each of these jobs costs less than a replacement garment. The shop is never empty, and her order book now runs two weeks ahead. She has taken on an apprentice of her own, convinced that the trade dies unless it is handed on aloud, with the hand on the work.

units: two clothes airers are sold in the same place at very different prices
the steel model opens easily and holds a heavy load
its feet slide on a smooth floor
the aluminium model weighs half as much
the aluminium model packs away in a narrow sleeve
its drying surface is smaller
the heavy one suits large households
the light one suits cramped homes
one corrodes at the joints and the other bows under a wet load
the decision turns on the space the buyer has at home
text: Two clothes airers stand side by side on the same shelf at prices far apart, and in use the gap tells less than the packaging promises. The first, in coated steel, opens out with a single movement and holds a heavy load without sagging. Its side wings lock on a firm catch, yet its feet slide on a smooth floor. The second, in aluminium, weighs half as much and packs away in a narrow sleeve, which is what suits a cramped flat. Its drying surface is smaller, and two sheets will barely fit on it. Put to the test, the heavy one serves a large household while the light one serves a small home. Neither deserves the enthusiasm of its leaflet: one corrodes at the folding joints, while the other bows its bars under a wet towel. What decides the matter, in the end, is the space the buyer has at home.

units: the writer of the message is going away and leaves instructions for the person sharing the flat
the kitchen tap drips if it is shut too quickly
a funnel for pouring oil sits under the sink
the wardrobe door has to be lifted before it will shut
a hanger has been freed up for a coat
the hot water takes a while before it can be used
the post box fills up quickly and has to be emptied
the recycling bag goes out at the start of the week
the neighbour below knocks on his ceiling when anyone walks heavily in the evening
that neighbour sleeps while the occupants are still up
text: Hello, I am off this evening, so here are the instructions for the flat, and I hope nothing is missing. Kitchen: the tap drips if you shut it too quickly, so turn it gently; the funnel for the oil sits under the sink, alongside the floor cloth. Bedroom: the wardrobe only closes if you lift the door while pushing, and I have freed a hanger for your coat. Bathroom: the hot water takes an age to come through, so switch it on before undressing. The post box fills quickly, so empty it on your way in and leave everything on the coffee table. The recycling bag goes out at the beginning of the week, so remember to take it down. One last thing: the neighbour below knocks on his ceiling whenever anyone walks heavily after supper. Take no offence, since he sleeps while we are still up.

units: a caretaker of a block of flats describes how his week goes
he starts at first light by cleaning the shared parts
he checks the lighting on the stairs
he wheels the bins out before the collection lorry comes
he brings the bins back washed once the collection is over
the bottom hinge on the door of the bike store gives way regularly
he straightens that door every other week
he sets aside a whole stretch of time for the repairs residents report
he makes a round at the end of the day to check that everything is locked
he reckons that the steadiness of the routine protects him
text: We asked the caretaker of a block of flats to take us through his week, task by task. He starts at first light with the shared parts: sweeping the entrance hall, running a mop over the floor, checking the bulbs on the stairs. Asked what comes next, he explains that he wheels the bins out before the lorry arrives and brings them back washed once it has gone. When we ask which fault returns most often, he names the door of the bike store, whose bottom hinge gives way under the weight and which he straightens every other week. Midweek he sets aside a whole stretch of time for the repairs residents have reported. Last comes the evening round, when he checks that everything is locked. Asked whether the work tires him, he answers that the routine protects him more than it wears him down.
